parsed.explanation: No trans-specific criminal offence, border/facility/custody restriction, or organised police targeting is documented, and same-sex conduct has been lawful since 1869 with the death penalty abolished. Courts have ruled for a trans applicant on marker change (2017, affirmed 2022) and the constitutional court called the Civil Code outdated (2023), signalling functioning, if slow, institutions. This is offset by documented daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation, implicit-only constitutional protection based on 'any other status', no comprehensive anti-discrimination law, uncertain whether hate-speech provisions cover gender identity, and a 2022 judgment whose execution was still being sought. No traveller-facing protection is documented as operating promptly. The combined regime is therefore moderately protective but with thin, delayed recourse and real social hostility.

entry_documents.interaction: No statutory marker-change procedure is resident-facing; no visitor document rejection is documented.

federal_state_facilities.interaction: No subnational variation documented; national-level findings only.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Daily discrimination, violence and stigmatisation of LGBTI people reported; enforcement and social conditions lag legal position.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Same-sex conduct lawful since 1869; 2015 penal provisions on sexual-orientation discrimination/hate speech; Employment Equal Treatment Act 2022 names gender identity; LGBTI organisations can register.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Hate-speech provisions' coverage of gender identity is uncertain, limiting stated protection for trans visitors.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Violence against LGBTI people reported in advocacy submission; trans-specific traveller incidents not documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Penal provisions punish sexual-orientation discrimination/hate speech up to one year or fine.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: No documented police protection or failure specific to trans visitors.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Marker recognition only via prolonged litigation; execution of 2022 appellate judgment still sought; no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute; coalition excluded from consultation.
remedies_unknowns.protection: First-instance 2017 and appellate 2022 rulings in favour of trans applicant; constitutional court 2023 urged Civil Code modernisation.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Court success shows recourse exists in principle but is slow and incomplete in execution, discounting paper protections.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar: protections exist and courts/a complaint route worked, but here remedies are slower and less prompt, and documented daily discrimination/violence is broader, so slightly lower than 0.65-A's apology/compensation outcome.

Higher than 0.55-B: no documented secondary screening, detention, entry refusal or discretionary border holding of trans visitors; the exposure here is social discrimination and weak recourse, not routine administrative detention.

Lower than 0.75-C: that anchor has explicit traveller entry acceptance, trained officers and a tribunal remedy; here traveller-facing acceptance and prompt remedies are not documented, and anti-discrimination coverage for gender identity remains implicit/partial.

parsed.synthesis: No documented traveller-facing criminalisation, universal-exposure measure, or organised targeting dominates the rating. The operative risk is Tier-3 societal hostility with thin recourse: daily discrimination/violence/stigmatisation amid implicit protections, a first gender-identity statute only in 2022, uncertain hate-speech coverage, and litigation-based recognition whose execution lagged. Mitigating this, decriminalisation since 1869, abolition of the death penalty, registrable LGBTI organisations, and courts ruling for trans litigants and criticising outdated law show institutions are not hostile perpetrators. Interaction is therefore law broadly tolerant but enforcement weak, placing the combined regime in Reduced Risk, below jurisdictions with documented working visitor protections.
